subject: antique camera photograph
title: The 5 Oldest Photographs Ever Taken, Ranked (#1 Took Hours to Expose)

scenes.text: The five oldest photographs on Earth, ranked. Number one needed at least eight hours of light.
Number five: 1840. John Draper photographs the Moon from a New York rooftop, the first clear picture of another world.
scenes.label: Draper Moon · 1840

scenes.text: Number four: 1839. Robert Cornelius runs in front of his own camera in Philadelphia and holds still for over a minute. The first selfie.
scenes.label: Cornelius selfie · 1839

scenes.text: Number three: 1838. Daguerre shoots a Paris boulevard. Minutes of exposure erase the traffic, except one man standing still for a boot shine. The first human ever photographed.
scenes.label: Paris boulevard · 1838

scenes.text: Number two: 1837. Daguerre's still life of plaster casts, the earliest reliably dated daguerreotype.
scenes.label: Daguerre still life · 1837

scenes.text: Number one: 1826 or 1827. Joseph Niépce aims a camera out of a window at a pewter plate coated in tar. Many hours later, maybe days, the oldest surviving photo exists.
scenes.label: Niépce window · 1826

description:
The five oldest surviving photographs, ranked by the year they were taken.
John Draper's 1840 daguerreotype of the Moon from New York University; Robert Cornelius's October 1839 self-portrait in Philadelphia, often called the first selfie; Louis Daguerre's 1838 Boulevard du Temple, where a man having his boots polished stood still long enough to become the first person ever photographed; Daguerre's 1837 still life of plaster casts, the earliest reliably dated daguerreotype; and Joseph Nicéphore Niépce's View from the Window at Le Gras, made in 1826 or 1827 on a pewter plate coated with bitumen with an exposure of many hours, now kept at the University of Texas at Austin.
Which of these would you most like to see in person, and what should we rank next?
first_comment: Which would you put at number one? The first photo of the Sun came in 1845, with sunspots visible in a 1/60th of a second exposure. What should we rank next?
